exact_title: Evaluating the Impact of Stair Climbing on Cardiovascular Risk Reduction: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
verification_notes: Verified against the primary paper (DOI 10.1007/s40256-026-00811-x, American Journal of Cardiovascular Drugs, 2026-08-13): title, journal, study design (systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies), sample composition, primary outcomes, main result, pooled effect sizes with CIs and p-values, major limitations, and funding statement all confirmed. pmid not yet assigned/found. Heterogeneity/sensitivity-analysis statistics referenced in the source were not fully re-verified during the prior audit and are treated as provisional rather than restated as confirmed figures. conflicts_of_interest is recorded strictly as 'no industry funding noted' per the source -- nothing broader is inferred. sample_size is recorded as the overall pooled total (480,479 participants across 9 studies); the mortality-specific subset (5 studies, 455,619 participants) is recorded separately in study_design rather than invented as a second sample_size field. headline_defensibility GREEN applies only to the replacement title below ('Stairs and Heart Death: The 39% Number Isn't What You Think'); an earlier causal-framed candidate headline was assessed RED and must not be restored.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. Overall pooled analysis: 9 studies, 480,479 total participants. Mortality-specific pooled analysis: 5 studies, 455,619 participants.
population: Adults approximately 35-84 years old across included observational cohorts.
main_result: Stair climbing was associated with lower cardiovascular mortality and lower all-cause mortality.
effect_size: Cardiovascular mortality: RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.48-0.79, p=0.0002. All-cause mortality: RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62-0.94, p=0.01.
p_value: Cardiovascular mortality: p=0.0002. All-cause mortality: p=0.01.
major_limitations: All underlying studies observational; healthy-user bias; reverse causation; self-reported activity in underlying studies; heterogeneity statistics were not fully verified during the prior audit.
funding: NIHR Academic Clinical Fellowships / Doctoral Research Fellowship
conflicts_of_interest: No industry funding noted; nothing beyond that is inferred.
why_now: Recently published evidence on a simple everyday behavior with broad public-health relevance, although the topic is primarily evergreen rather than tied to a breaking event.
provisional_fields: statistical_robustness (sensitivity analysis / heterogeneity component not fully verified)
proposed_title: Stairs and Heart Death: The 39% Number Isn't What You Think
thumbnail_text: 39% LOWER HEART-DEATH RISK — BUT IS IT THE STAIRS?
best_video_angle: Use the study to explain why a very large observational association can still fail to establish causation.
